title: Handle and store fuel safely
summary: Petrol, diesel and propane are among the first supplies looted and the most dangerous to handle. Move fuel with a pump, never your mouth; store it outdoors in proper containers; keep sparks and static away; and learn to spot fuel that has gone bad.

materials.item: Hand transfer pump or self-priming siphon hose
Proper fuel cans with tight caps
Funnel and a clean cloth or filter
Clear glass jar for checking fuel
Fire extinguisher, bucket of sand or fire blanket
Leak-detection solution, or chloride-free soap and water, in a spray bottle, for gas leak checks

steps.text: Work outdoors, upwind, away from flames, running engines and anyone smoking. Have the extinguisher or sand ready.

Check fuel before you take it. Pour a little into a clear glass jar and let it settle (Alberta farm fuel). Good petrol is clear and light. Stale petrol is darker and smells sour or like varnish. Water and sludge sink to the bottom as a separate layer.
Move fuel with a hand pump or a self-priming siphon. Many newer cars have a valve or screen that stops a hose reaching the tank; don't force it.
steps.warn: Never start a siphon by mouth (CCOHS fuel). Fuel in the lungs causes a severe pneumonia that can kill.

steps.text: At petrol stations, the underground tanks have fill points under round covers on the forecourt. Pump from them with a long hose and a hand pump, keeping the end of the hose clear of the bottom so you don't pull up water and sludge.
steps.warn: Tank openings hold heavy vapour. No sparks, and don't put your face over the opening.

steps.text: Put cans on the ground to fill them, never in a vehicle or on a plastic liner. Keep the nozzle touching the can so static can't spark (CCOHS fuel, Manitoba gas cans).
Leave about 5% of each can empty for expansion (CCOHS fuel), close it tightly and wipe off spills.
Store fuel in a shaded, ventilated shed or outdoor store, away from living spaces, wells and streams.

Keep propane cylinders upright and outdoors (RBQ propane), with the valve closed when not in use (BC propane). Check every connection with a leak-detection solution, or chloride-free soap and water (Goodman IO-359J): growing bubbles mean a leak. Rinse it off afterwards, because some soaps corrode some metals (Lennox EL297UHV).
steps.warn: Propane is heavier than air (RBQ propane) and pools in basements, pits and low ground.

steps.text: Let engines cool before refuelling. Never refuel a running engine or a hot generator.
steps.warn: Petrol spilled on a hot exhaust can ignite.

steps.text: Use the oldest fuel first. Add stabiliser to fresh fuel if you have it, and label cans with the date.

notes:
## Shelf life

| Fuel | Rough life, sealed and cool | Signs it has gone off |
|---|---|---|
| Petrol | about 6 months at best, kept cool in a nearly full, sealed container; Alberta says to use it within a month of buying where you can (Alberta farm fuel). A stabiliser may stretch that to about 15 months, but ELGAS gives no source for the figure (ELGAS shelf life). Small engines want it fresher: see below | gummy or varnish-like deposits, water or sediment in the jar, hard starting (Alberta farm fuel, ELGAS shelf life) |
| Stihl MotoMix (ethanol-free, premixed with synthetic oil) | up to 2 years (Stihl fuel) | none given |
| Diesel | 6–12 months if kept clean, cool and dry (Alberta farm fuel). ELGAS quotes BP as 12 months or more at about 20 °C and 6–12 months above 30 °C, and says 3 years or more with a stabiliser containing antioxidant and biocide, without saying who measured that (ELGAS shelf life) | gummy deposits, sediment, slime or sludge; dark and layered (ELGAS shelf life); water in the tank (Alberta farm fuel) |
| Kerosene (paraffin) for a heater | no more than 6 months; start each heating season with fresh fuel (Toyotomi KS-27A) | yellow, cloudy or sour-smelling; water or dirt in it (Toyotomi KS-27A) |
| Propane | doesn't go off; the cylinder is the limit (ELGAS shelf life) | rusty, dented or damaged cylinder. BC says to replace or re-qualify one more than 10 years old (BC propane); Quebec says never to fill one over 10 years old (RBQ propane) |

These are rough. Heat, big temperature swings, air and water make fuel go off faster (Alberta farm fuel, ELGAS shelf life).
- **Small engines:** Stihl says not to use petrol older than 60 days, and preferably not older than 30, even with stabiliser (Stihl fuel). Honda tells snow-blower owners to add stabiliser if a can will take more than 3 months to use up, and not to leave petrol, stabilised or not, in the machine unused for more than 90 days (Honda fuel).
- **Stabiliser** can slow the oxidation of fresh fuel (ELGAS shelf life) but won't bring stale fuel back (Honda fuel).
- **Bad kerosene** gives a low flame, tar on the wick, smoke and smell, and makes the heater hard to light or put out. Rapid, heavy tar build-up can mean poor or deteriorated fuel (Toyotomi KS-27A).

## Vapour

Petrol vapour burns when it makes up only about 1.4–7.6% of the air (NIOSH gasoline), so a small spill in a closed room can be enough. The vapour is heavier than air, drifts to low places and can travel a long way to an ignition source (CCOHS fuel). Pilot lights, heaters and switches are the usual ones.

## Static

Fuel flowing through a hose builds static charge. Never fill a can in a car boot or a pickup bed: on a plastic bed liner the charge can't drain away, and a spark can light the fumes (Manitoba gas cans). On the ground, the charge drains away.

## Wrong fuel

- Petrol in a diesel engine can wreck it.
- Diesel in a petrol engine stops it running.
- Two-stroke engines (chainsaws, trimmers, many outboards) need oil mixed into the petrol. The ratio is usually on the tank cap or in the manual.

## Common mistakes

- Filling cans in a truck bed.
- Storing a fuel can inside the house.
- Using petrol to start a fire.
- Topping up a hot generator.
- Storing propane in a basement or tent.
